title: UNIT 6: ELECTRICITY
notes:
✓ Charge → Produces electric force and electric fields.

✓ Potential difference → Provides the driving effect for current.

✓ Current → Movement of charge through a conductor.

✓ Resistance → Opposes current.

✓ Capacitor → Stores electric charge and electrical energy.

title: 6.1 ELECTRIC CHARGES
notes:
✓ Electric charge → A fundamental property of matter responsible for electrical interactions.

◆ TYPES OF CHARGE
✓ Positive charge → Associated with loss of electrons.
✓ Negative charge → Associated with gain of electrons.
✓ Like charges → Repel.
✓ Unlike charges → Attract.

◆ PROPERTIES OF ELECTRIC CHARGE
✓ Conservation → Charge cannot be created or destroyed; it is transferred from one body to another.

✓ Quantization → Charge occurs in integral multiples of the elementary charge:
q = ±ne

✓ n = 1, 2, 3, ...
✓ e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C

✓ Additivity → Total charge of a system is the algebraic sum of individual charges.

◆ COULOMB’S LAW
✓ Electrostatic force → Is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation:
F = k|q₁q₂|/r²

✓ k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²

✓ Vector form:
F⃗₁₂ = k(q₁q₂/r²)r̂₁₂

◆ DIRECTION
✓ Like charges → Repulsive force.
✓ Unlike charges → Attractive force.
✓ Force → Acts along the line joining the two charges.

◆ SUPERPOSITION PRINCIPLE
✓ For several charges → Net force is the vector sum of all individual forces:
F⃗net = F⃗₁ + F⃗₂ + F⃗₃ + ...

✓ Doubling the separation → Reduces the electrostatic force to one-fourth.

✓ F ∝ 1/r²

✓ Electrostatic force → Is enormously stronger than gravitational force at the atomic scale.

title: 6.2 ELECTRIC FIELDS
notes:
✓ Electric field → The region around a charged object in which another charge experiences an electric force.

◆ ELECTRIC FIELD STRENGTH
✓ Electric field strength → Force per unit positive test charge:
E⃗ = F⃗/q

✓ Unit → N/C or V/m.

✓ For a point charge:
E = k|Q|/r²

✓ Direction → Away from a positive charge and toward a negative charge.

◆ FORCE ON A CHARGE IN A FIELD
✓ F⃗ = qE⃗

✓ Positive charge → Experiences force in the direction of E⃗.

✓ Negative charge → Experiences force opposite to E⃗.

◆ ELECTRIC FIELD LINES
✓ Begin on positive charges and terminate on negative charges.
✓ Never cross one another.
✓ Are perpendicular to the surface of a charged conductor.
✓ Closer lines → Indicate a stronger field.
✓ Equally spaced parallel lines → Represent a uniform electric field.

◆ COMMON FIELD PATTERNS
✓ Single positive charge → Radial outward lines.
✓ Single negative charge → Radial inward lines.
✓ Electric dipole → Lines from + to −.
✓ Oppositely charged parallel plates → Approximately uniform field between plates.

◆ UNIFORM ELECTRIC FIELD
✓ For parallel plates:
E = ΔV/d

✓ ΔV → Potential difference.
✓ d → Plate separation.

◆ ELECTRIC FLUX
✓ Electric flux → Measures the amount of electric field passing through a surface.

✓ Φ = EA cosθ

✓ For a uniform field perpendicular to the surface:
Φ = EA

✓ Unit → N·m²/C.

◆ MULTIPLE CHARGES
✓ Resultant electric field → Is the vector sum of the fields produced by individual charges:
E⃗net = E⃗₁ + E⃗₂ + E⃗₃ + ...

✓ Key idea → Electric field is a property of the region created by source charges; force is the effect experienced by a charge placed in that field.

title: 6.3 ELECTRIC POTENTIAL
notes:
✓ Electric potential → Describes the electric potential energy available per unit charge at a point.

◆ ELECTRIC POTENTIAL ENERGY
✓ Electric potential energy → Depends on the position of a charge in an electric field.

✓ For two point charges:
U = kq₁q₂/r

◆ ELECTRIC POTENTIAL
✓ V = U/q

✓ For a point charge:
V = kQ/r

✓ Electric potential → Is a scalar quantity.

✓ Unit → Volt (V) = joule/coulomb (J/C).

◆ POTENTIAL DIFFERENCE
✓ Potential difference → Change in electric potential between two points and work done per unit charge:
ΔV = W/q

✓ For a uniform electric field:
ΔV = Ed

✓ This magnitude relation applies when displacement is along the field.

◆ ELECTRIC FIELD & POTENTIAL
✓ Electric field → Points in the direction of decreasing electric potential.

✓ Stronger potential gradient → Corresponds to a stronger electric field.

◆ EMF
✓ Electromotive force (emf) → Energy supplied by a source per unit charge.

✓ Unit → Volt.

◆ EQUIPOTENTIAL SURFACES/LINES
✓ Equipotential lines or surfaces → Connect points having the same electric potential.

✓ Moving a charge along an equipotential → Requires no work.
✓ Equipotential surfaces → Never intersect.
✓ Equipotential surfaces → Are perpendicular to electric field lines.
✓ Point charge → Has concentric spherical equipotential surfaces.
✓ Uniform field → Has parallel equipotential surfaces.

✓ Key idea → Potential → Energy per unit charge.

✓ Potential difference → Work/energy transferred per unit charge.

✓ Electric field → Force per unit charge.

title: 6.4 ELECTRIC CURRENT, RESISTANCE AND OHM’S LAW
notes:
✓ Electric current → Rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor.

◆ ELECTRIC CURRENT
✓ I = ΔQ/Δt

✓ For steady current:
I = Q/t

✓ SI unit → Ampere (A).

✓ 1 A = 1 C/s.

◆ CURRENT DENSITY
✓ Current density → Current per unit cross-sectional area:
J = I/A

✓ Unit → A/m².

◆ DRIFT VELOCITY
✓ Drift velocity → Average directed velocity acquired by charge carriers in a conductor due to an electric field.

✓ I = nqAvd

✓ n → Number density of charge carriers.
✓ q → Charge of each carrier.
✓ A → Cross-sectional area.
✓ vd → Drift velocity.

◆ RESISTANCE
✓ Resistance → Opposition a conductor offers to electric current.

✓ R = V/I

✓ Unit → Ohm (Ω).

✓ One ohm → Resistance through which a current of 1 A flows when the potential difference is 1 V.

◆ RESISTIVITY
✓ Resistance of a uniform conductor:
R = ρL/A

✓ ρ → Resistivity.

✓ Unit → Ω·m.

✓ Conductivity → Reciprocal of resistivity:
σ = 1/ρ

✓ Unit → S/m.

◆ TEMPERATURE EFFECT
✓ Metallic conductors → Resistance generally increases as temperature increases.

✓ Semiconductors → Generally show decreasing resistance with increasing temperature.

✓ Superconductors → Can exhibit essentially zero electrical resistance below a critical temperature.

◆ OHM’S LAW
✓ For an ohmic conductor at constant physical conditions:
V = IR

✓ V–I graph for an ohmic conductor → Straight line through the origin.

◆ SERIES CONNECTION
✓ Rs = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + ...

✓ Same current → Flows through every resistor.
✓ Voltage → Divides among resistors.
✓ Total resistance → Is greater than any individual resistance.

◆ PARALLEL CONNECTION
✓ 1/Rp = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ + ...

✓ Same potential difference → Across each branch.
✓ Current → Divides among branches.
✓ Equivalent resistance → Is less than the smallest branch resistance.

◆ ELECTRIC POWER
✓ P = VI = I²R = V²/R

✓ Electrical energy:
W = Pt

◆ RESISTOR COLOR CODE
✓ Resistor bands → Indicate resistance value and tolerance.

✓ First bands → Give significant digits.
✓ Next band → Gives the multiplier.
✓ Tolerance band → Gives the allowed variation.

◆ CELLS, EMF AND INTERNAL RESISTANCE
✓ A real cell → Has internal resistance r.

✓ Terminal voltage while supplying current:
V = ε − Ir

✓ Current in a simple circuit:
I = ε/(R + r)

✓ ε → Emf.
✓ R → External resistance.
✓ r → Internal resistance.

✓ Key idea → EMF is the energy supplied per unit charge by a source, while terminal voltage is the potential difference available at the terminals under operating conditions.

title: 6.4 ELECTRICAL MEASURING INSTRUMENTS & CIRCUITS
notes:
◆ AMMETER
✓ Ammeter → Measures electric current and is connected in series.
✓ Its resistance → Should be very small.

◆ VOLTMETER
✓ Voltmeter → Measures potential difference and is connected in parallel.
✓ Its resistance → Should be very large.

◆ GALVANOMETER
✓ Galvanometer → A sensitive instrument used to detect and measure small electric currents.

✓ Galvanometer → Can be converted into an ammeter by connecting a suitable low-resistance shunt in parallel.

✓ Galvanometer → Can be converted into a voltmeter by connecting a high resistance in series.

◆ POTENTIOMETER
✓ Potentiometer → Uses the potential drop along a uniform resistance wire to measure or compare potential differences.

◆ APPLICATIONS
Measuring emf of a cell.
Measuring internal resistance of a cell.
Comparing emf of cells.
Acting as a variable resistor.

◆ WHEATSTONE BRIDGE
✓ Wheatstone bridge → Used to determine an unknown resistance by balancing two branches of a circuit.

✓ At balance → No current flows through the galvanometer.

✓ Standard balanced bridge:
R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄

◆ KIRCHHOFF’S FIRST LAW — JUNCTION RULE
✓ Total current entering a junction → Equals total current leaving it:
ΣIin = ΣIout

✓ Junction rule → Follows from conservation of charge.

◆ KIRCHHOFF’S SECOND LAW — LOOP RULE
✓ Algebraic sum of potential changes around any closed loop → Is zero:
ΣΔV = 0

✓ Loop rule → Follows from conservation of energy.

◆ CIRCUIT-SOLVING STEPS
✓ Assume directions for branch currents.
✓ Apply the junction rule.
✓ Apply the loop rule to independent loops.
✓ Solve the simultaneous equations.
✓ Negative current → Means the actual direction is opposite to the assumed direction.

✓ Key idea → Junction rule → Conservation of charge.

✓ Loop rule → Conservation of energy.

title: 6.4 SERIES & PARALLEL BULBS
notes:
✓ Light bulbs → Behave as electrical loads, and their brightness depends on the electrical power delivered to them.

◆ SERIES BULBS
✓ Same current → Flows through every bulb.
✓ Supply voltage → Is divided.
✓ Adding bulbs → Increases total resistance and generally reduces current.
✓ Bulbs → Are affected by one another because they share the same current path.

◆ PARALLEL BULBS
✓ Same potential difference → Is applied across each branch.
✓ Total current → Divides among branches.
✓ Each bulb → Can operate independently.
✓ Adding another parallel branch → Changes the total current drawn from the source.

◆ PRACTICAL IDEA
✓ Household loads → Are connected mainly in parallel so each appliance receives the supply voltage and can operate independently.

title: 6.6 CAPACITORS AND CAPACITANCE
notes:
✓ Capacitor → A device consisting of conductors separated by an insulating material and used to store electric charge and electrical energy.

◆ CAPACITANCE
✓ Capacitance → Measures the ability of a capacitor to store charge:
C = Q/V

✓ Unit → Farad (F).

✓ 1 F = 1 C/V.

◆ PARALLEL-PLATE CAPACITOR
✓ For two parallel conducting plates:
C = ε₀A/d

✓ A → Plate area.
✓ d → Separation.

✓ Larger plate area → Larger capacitance.
✓ Smaller separation → Larger capacitance.

◆ DIELECTRIC
✓ Dielectric → An insulating material placed between capacitor plates.

✓ Dielectric → Increases capacitance:
C = kC₀

✓ k → Dielectric constant.
✓ C₀ → Capacitance without the dielectric.

◆ EFFECT OF DIELECTRIC
✓ If the capacitor remains connected to the source:
C increases.
V remains constant.
Q increases.
Stored energy increases.

✓ If the capacitor is isolated:
C increases.
Q remains constant.
V decreases.
Electric field decreases.

◆ DIELECTRIC STRENGTH
✓ Dielectric strength → Maximum electric field a dielectric can withstand before electrical breakdown occurs.

◆ ENERGY STORED IN A CAPACITOR
✓ U = ½CV²

✓ Equivalent forms:
U = ½QV = Q²/(2C)

◆ CAPACITORS IN PARALLEL
✓ Ceq = C₁ + C₂ + C₃ + ...

✓ Same voltage → Across each capacitor.

✓ Charges add:
Qtotal = Q₁ + Q₂ + Q₃ + ...

◆ CAPACITORS IN SERIES
✓ 1/Ceq = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + 1/C₃ + ...

✓ Same magnitude of charge → On each capacitor.
✓ Voltage → Divides among the capacitors.

◆ APPLICATIONS
Energy storage.
Electronic circuits.
Timing circuits.
Filtering and signal processing.
Starting certain electric motors.
Camera flashes and other pulse-energy applications.

✓ Key idea → Capacitor → Stores charge and energy.

✓ C = Q/V → Larger C means more charge can be stored for the same voltage.

title: 6.7 ELECTRIC CIRCUITS IN OUR SURROUNDINGS
notes:
✓ Household electrical installations → Apply electric-circuit principles to safely distribute electrical energy to appliances.

◆ HOUSEHOLD CIRCUITS
✓ Household appliances → Are generally connected in parallel so that:

✓ Each appliance → Receives the supply potential difference.
✓ Appliances → Can be switched independently.
✓ Failure of one branch → Does not normally stop other branches.

◆ COMMON ELECTRICAL LOADS
Lighting systems.
Electric heaters.
Kettles.
Refrigerators.
Television and electronic devices.
Washing machines and other appliances.

◆ ELECTRICAL SAFETY
✓ Safe installations → Require appropriate protection against excessive current, short circuits and accidental contact with dangerous conductors.

◆ CIRCUIT PROTECTION
✓ Fuses and circuit breakers → Interrupt a circuit when current becomes dangerously large.

◆ EARTHING/GROUNDING
✓ Earthing → Provides a low-resistance path for fault current and helps reduce the danger of electric shock when a fault makes a metal appliance casing live.

◆ SMART ELECTRICAL SYSTEMS
✓ Modern electrical installations → Can incorporate automated control, monitoring and smart-house technologies to manage electrical appliances and energy use.

✓ Key idea → Household wiring applies series/parallel circuit principles, electrical measurements, protection and safe energy distribution.
